assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
Asking more than one person for advice is a good way to make a better decision. I think this because nobody can see a problem from every side, and one person might miss something important.

Say a girl is trying to pick between two colleges. Her parents might care the most about the price and how far away the school is. Her teacher might tell her that one school has a better program for the subject she likes. Her cousin goes to one of the schools, so he can tell her what it is really like, like the dorms being crowded and how cold it gets in winter.

Another reason is that people are biased. Everyone giving advice has their own life and their own wants, and that changes what they say. A mom might want her kid to stay close to home, and a friend might want someone to hang out with at the same school. But if a bunch of different people who don't know each other all say the same thing, it is easier to trust them. If they disagree, then she knows the choice is hard, and she can take her time and think about what matters most to her.

Disagreement is also helpful because it makes you explain why you think what you think. Say one person tells you to take the safe job and another person says to take the risk. Now you have to figure out which worries are real for you. Doing that can show you what you really care about.

The choice is still yours, and too many opinions can get confusing. But a few good ones can help you pick.
essay_2:
I think asking more than one person for advice is a smart way to make a choice. One person can't see a problem from every side, and that is the main reason it helps.

Say a girl is picking between two colleges. Her parents might worry about the cost and how far away it is. Her teacher might say one school has a strong program for the subject she likes. Her cousin goes to one of the schools and can tell her what it is like, even the bad parts like the crowded dorms and the cold winters. Each person knows something the others don't. When she puts it all together, she gets a bigger picture than she would from one talk.

Another reason is bias. Every adviser has their own wants and worries. A mom might want her kid to stay home, but a friend might want company. If several people who don't know each other say the same thing, she can trust it more. If they disagree, she learns the choice is hard, so she can slow down and think about what matters to her. That isn't a bad thing.

Disagreement also helps because it makes her explain her own reasons. If one person says take the safe job and another says take the risk, she has to figure out which fears are real. That is a way to find out what she values. It takes a little more time to ask around, and some answers will be hard to hear.

Of course, the choice still belongs to her, and too many voices can get confusing. However, a few caring opinions, weighed with care, can help a person avoid mistakes and feel happy about a great decision.
